b18270f562:
This chapter is about trust, in two settings.

In the extraction scenario, the question is how much model output you can use without a person checking it. The answer has to come from per-type, per-field evidence, not a headline number.

In the research scenario, the question is whether a reader can trace every claim to its source after several agents have summarised it.

The chapter builds the measurement (stratified sampling, calibration, thresholds, routing, audit) and the data model (claim records that survive every hand-off). The runnable code uses synthetic data, labelled as such.
9519fbada6:
Never decide to automate on an aggregate accuracy number: measure accuracy per document type and per field with stratified random samples, calibrate any confidence score against labelled data from your own documents, and send low-confidence, high-stakes or validation-failing items to people.

Never let attribution travel as prose: carry structured claim-to-source records (with dates, quotes and methods) through every agent hand-off, merge them without erasing disagreement, and keep established, contested and single-source findings visibly apart.
c62d557db4:
The two halves are the same problem, seen from either side of a human.

In 5.5, a person sits downstream of the model and must be pointed at the items most likely to be wrong. In 5.6, a person sits at the end of a pipeline and must be able to check a claim they doubt.

In both, the system's job is to expose its own uncertainty and its own evidence as data. It shouldn't hide them in an average or in smooth prose.
dd22fbba8f:
The official knowledge points for 5.5:

  • the risk that aggregate accuracy (for example 97% overall) masks poor performance on specific document types or fields;
  • stratified random sampling for measuring error rates and detecting novel error patterns;
  • field-level confidence scores calibrated with labelled validation sets;
  • the need to analyse accuracy by document type and field before automating.

For 5.6:

  • source attribution is lost during summarisation when findings are compressed without claim-source mappings;
  • the structural need for claim-source mappings preserved and merged by the synthesis step;
  • how to handle conflicting statistics (annotate both values with attribution, do not pick one);
  • the importance of publication and collection dates;
  • coverage and conflict presented in a structured way;
  • rendering different content types appropriately (financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists).
69fa3553c9:
Inspecting every item is slow and expensive. Inspecting a random sample, and deciding about the lot from it, is the foundation of industrial quality control.

Walter Shewhart's control charts at Bell Labs in the 1920s tracked a process over time, to separate normal variation from a real shift. The Dodge and Romig sampling plans (also Bell Labs, 1920s and 1930s) turned the idea into tables. Given a lot size and an acceptable defect rate, they said how many items to inspect and how many defects justify rejecting the lot. The war-time Military Standard 105 made acceptance sampling routine.

Two ideas from this tradition are the ones the exam tests. A sample must be random within its stratum, or it's biased by whoever chose it. And a lot made of mixed parts should be stratified, so that each part is measured.

The post-launch audit in this chapter is a control chart in spirit: a continuing sample that tells you when the process has shifted.
ccfd3d17bf:
Jerzy Neyman's 1934 paper on sampling made the case for stratified random sampling and optimal allocation. Split the population into homogeneous strata, sample within each, and weight the results back by true population share. Pollsters use it so that a small subgroup (a minority of voters, a rare document type) is measured precisely enough to say anything, without paying to over-sample everything.

The confidence interval is the companion idea. A sample proportion of 77% from 22 items is compatible with anything from about 57% to 90%. That's why the rare-type estimate from a simple random sample can't support a decision.

The code uses Wilson's 1927 interval, because it behaves sensibly at small n and near 0 and 1.
4825feeacf:
A probability forecast is calibrated if events it says happen 70% of the time do happen about 70% of the time. Meteorologists formalised this in the 1950s (Brier's score, 1950; reliability diagrams). The field of forecast verification has been checking weather forecasts against outcomes ever since.

Machine learning rediscovered the problem when deep networks turned out to be systematically miscalibrated (Guo et al., 2017, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks"). The standard fixes (temperature scaling, histogram binning, isotonic regression) all do the same thing. They learn, from labelled held-out data, the map from score to observed accuracy.

For language models, the same issue applies to any confidence a model states about its own output. Whether a stated number tracks correctness is an empirical property of a model, a task and a distribution. The number itself doesn't imply it. The exam's phrase is "calibrated using labelled validation sets", and that is the whole method.
9a8a0cab40:
Systems that defer hard cases to people have a long record in telecom and finance: fraud queues, call-centre escalation. Machine learning has a formal name for it, selective prediction or "learning to reject" (Chow, 1957, on the error-reject trade-off).

The central object is the risk-coverage curve. As you automate more (higher coverage), the error rate on the automated part rises. Setting a threshold means choosing a point on that curve. The review capacity table in this chapter is that curve with reviewer hours attached.
5b14db04b5:
Provenance, the record of where a thing came from, matured in several fields independently:

  • archivists and historians use citation and chain-of-custody;
  • library science has bibliographic standards;
  • databases developed data lineage, meaning which source rows produced this output row (Buneman, Khanna and Tan's 2001 work on "why and where" provenance);
  • the W3C published PROV (2013) as a standard model;
  • scientific publishing formalised the claim and its evidence through citations.

The lesson common to all of them: attribution kept as a first-class field survives transformation, and attribution kept in a sentence doesn't. A summary is a transformation. So a summary that doesn't carry the mapping loses it.

Journalism has the same rule in a sharper form. A number without a source and a date isn't yet a fact. And when two sources disagree, the story reports the disagreement.
65c472067c:
Begin with the decision that a measurement feeds. For extraction, the decision is "which records can the business act on without human review".

The cost of being wrong isn't the average error rate. It's the cost of the specific wrong records that get through. That depends on the type: a wrong tower-lease escalation date costs something different from a wrong utility meter reading. It also depends on the field: a wrong vendor name is a nuisance, while a wrong bank account is a fraud. A single average can't see any of this.

The average also hides how averages mislead. A population is a mixture, and the average of a mixture is dominated by its largest component. The 97% in the running example is 70% invoices at 99.2%, mixed with 5% handwritten receipts at around 72%. The headline is true, and useless for the decision about receipts.
13704c789c:
Second, what a confidence score is for. A score exists to let you split items into those you'll accept without review and those you won't. For that, it needs two properties:

  • It must rank: errors should score lower than correct answers, on average.
  • It must be calibrated enough that a threshold on it has a known meaning (above 0.9 means about 98% correct, on this type).

Ranking can be good while calibration is poor. Calibration can hold on average while failing on a segment.

The measurement that checks both is the reliability table. Bin items by score, compute observed accuracy in each bin, and compare. That table has to be computed per document type, on labelled data from your distribution. The relationship between score and correctness is a property of the segment.
5d123b3e6b:
Third, why provenance is a data-model problem rather than a prompting problem.

Asking an agent to "include citations" works while it still has the sources in its context. But say a subagent summarises its sources into prose and hands that prose to a synthesis agent. The synthesis agent can only cite what the prose contains, and the prose contains the claim, not the evidence. No instruction to the synthesiser can recover information that isn't in its input.

The fix is upstream. Make the hand-off format carry a record per claim, with fields for source, date and quote, and have every later stage preserve the record. The test of the design is mechanical: for every number in the final report, can code find the claim record that produced it?
53cb9de63f: Suppose a carrier extracts fields from four document types for its accounts-payable team: supplier invoices, tower-lease statements, utility bills for cell sites, and scanned handwritten field-service receipts. An evaluation on 1,000 random documents reports 97% field accuracy. The project lead proposes turning off human review.
b8983c3736:
The 97% is real, and it's the wrong number to decide on. Handwritten receipts are 5% of volume and nearly half the errors. One in four of their fields is wrong. Tower leases, with renewal dates and escalation clauses, are at 93%.

The same averaging happens across fields. vendor_name may be 99.9% while tax_amount is 91%. A single aggregate is a weighted average, dominated by the easy, high-volume case.
c054cd5de6: An architect will recognise this from SLOs. A 99.9% overall success rate on an API can hide a single endpoint failing 20% of the time for one large customer. So you slice by endpoint and tenant. Here you slice by document type and by field.
0679c7df10:
The rule from the objective: measure accuracy per document type (and per field) before automating, and automate type by type.

In the example, digital supplier invoices might go to automatic posting with sampled audits. Utility bills might be automated for most fields, with human review for amounts above a threshold. Tower leases and handwritten receipts stay in full human review until their accuracy improves.
0544d4b163: Review only low-confidence items. You learn nothing about the errors the model was confident about. Those are the ones that reach production unseen.
306b7fd997: Simple random sample of everything. With 70% supplier invoices, a 200-item sample contains about 10 handwritten receipts. That's too few to estimate their error rate.
8519d35605:
Stratified random sampling splits the population into strata (document type, and confidence band within type). It samples each stratum separately, at a rate chosen for that stratum.

Small, risky strata get enough samples to measure. High-confidence auto-approved items still get sampled, so silent errors become visible.
44e836d938: If you need a single number, weight each stratum's result by its true volume to report back to the overall population. Keep the per-stratum table as the decision tool.
61eb5400eb:
The Wilson interval shows why stratification isn't optional.

Take the companion's synthetic population and a 500-document simple random sample. The 22 handwritten receipts that land in the sample give 77% accuracy, with a 95% interval of about 57% to 90%. With 125 per stratum, the same type gives 70%, with an interval of about 62% to 78%. For the type you most need to know about, the estimate has gone from "could be anything" to "clearly not ready". The cost is the same 500 reviews.

A rough planning rule: the half-width of a 95% interval on a proportion near p is about 2·sqrt(p(1-p)/n). So knowing a 98% accuracy to within ±2 points takes roughly 200 items. Knowing a 99.5% accuracy to within ±0.5 points takes on the order of 800.

Targets near 100% need much bigger samples to verify than targets near 80%. That's a reason to state the target before sampling.
456befb3f7: Estimating the overall number from a stratified sample takes one more step. Weight each stratum's accuracy by its true share of volume (example 02 prints the volume-weighted overall). That keeps the headline unbiased, while the per-stratum table carries the decision.
859418b537:
A confidence score is calibrated if, among all fields scored about 0.9, about 90% are correct. Raw model-reported confidence isn't calibrated by default. A model asked to rate its certainty may say 0.95 for most fields, wrong ones included. That's why Chapter 14 rejected self-reported confidence as an escalation trigger.

The difference here is the next step. You measure how the score relates to correctness on a labelled validation set, then choose thresholds from that measurement. Once you know what each level actually means for each field and document type, the score becomes useful as a ranking signal.
03103edf7e:
Ask for confidence per field as part of the structured extraction (task 4.3, Chapter 12). Use a tool schema where each field has a value and a confidence, plus an evidence quote.

The evidence quote does two jobs. A reviewer can check it in seconds. And it pushes the model to ground the value in text.
ca03595491: Take a labelled set of a few hundred documents per type, with ground truth from human review. Run extraction. For each field and type, find the lowest threshold at which the items scoring above it meet the required accuracy. Record how much volume that leaves for automation.
1d16657d4b: Note the None outcome. For handwritten receipts, there may be no threshold at which tax_amount reaches 99%. That's a legitimate answer. The field stays in human review, and the data tells you where to invest: better scans, a different prompt, few-shot examples for that layout.
df7474753e: The reviewer sees only the uncertain fields with their evidence quotes, not the whole document to re-key. That's what makes partial automation pay. The human handles 2 fields out of 12 on a small share of documents, instead of all 12 on every one.
5da7d44aca:
The section above defines calibration. This section runs it.

Companion example 03 builds a reliability table on a synthetic validation set. It bins by score, then computes the mean score and the observed accuracy in each bin. The gap in each bin is the calibration error. Weighted by bin size, it gives the expected calibration error (ECE), which was 0.039 on the synthetic data. On this data, the score isn't wildly off on average. A reader who stopped at the ECE would conclude it's fine.

Example 07 then splits by document type, and that's where the problem shows. A raw score of 0.96 corresponds to about 100% observed accuracy on invoices, 98% on tower leases, and only 75% on handwritten receipts. The same number carries three different meanings.

The average calibration hides the segment. It's the aggregate-masks-segment problem of section 03 appearing a second time, in the confidence layer.
59f1b1de95:
Example 04 fits a threshold per type on a validation set. It scans upwards until observed accuracy among accepted items reaches the target: 98% in the demo, with a floor of 200 accepted items so a tiny lucky bin can't qualify. Then it applies the threshold to a separate held-out set.

Three results from the run are worth stating.

  • Invoices clear the target at any threshold, so they're automated almost completely.
  • Tower leases need a threshold of 0.98, and then only about 26% of leases qualify.
  • Handwritten receipts never reach the target at any threshold, so the policy is "always human review". That's a legitimate outcome of the method, not a failure of it.

And on the held-out set, utility bills accept 99% of items at 97.7% accuracy, slightly under the 98% fitted on validation. Validation estimates are optimistic by about their sampling error. That's why the held-out check and the post-launch audit exist.
e9a3cf778a: These numbers come from seeded synthetic data (example 04 prints them). The table is a template for your own, not a finding about any model.
4b07380d68:
A threshold also fixes how much work lands on the review team. Example 06 sweeps the threshold on the synthetic 40,000-document month, assuming 2.5 minutes per review (an assumption you should replace).

  • At threshold 0.85, 89% of items are automated, about 180 reviewer hours are needed, and about 756 wrong items a month get through automatically.
  • At 0.95, 44% are automated, about 938 hours are needed, and 249 wrong items get through.

The residual error never reaches zero, because some wrong answers score high. The table makes the trade explicit: the choice is between reviewer hours and wrong automatic items. The architect's job is to put both columns in front of the business owner, not a single threshold.
66291b1b42:
Everything above assumes the population stays the same. It doesn't. A supplier changes its invoice layout, a new OCR vendor comes in, a model version is upgraded (Chapter 18 covers pinning).

Example 08 simulates five months in which true accuracy drifts down from 99.5% to 88%. A weekly random audit of 400 auto-accepted items, with a Wilson interval, raises an alert in month 4, when the upper bound falls below the 98% target.

The audit must be a random sample of the auto-accepted population. Not of low-confidence items, and not of items a reviewer happened to open; otherwise it measures the wrong population. And the review UI shouldn't tell the reviewer which items are audit items. If it does, the audit measures how reviewers treat flagged items, not what the model did.
0a4463f0e4:
Routing is a function from an extracted record to a queue. The confidence threshold is one input. Example 05 shows the order that holds up in practice:

  1. First, hard validation failures force review regardless of confidence: a calculated total that differs from the stated total, a date in the future, a currency code not in the allowed list (Chapter 12 covers semantic validation).
  2. Second, policy by document type: if the type hasn't been approved for automation, everything is reviewed.
  3. Third, confidence thresholds per field, with a margin added for high-stakes fields such as bank account or total amount.

Only an item that passes all three is auto-accepted.

Why this order? The first two are deterministic and auditable. The third rests on a statistical estimate. So the estimate gets to say "yes" only where nothing deterministic says "no".
896229c40a: Return the reasons, not just the decision. They tell the reviewer what to look at. They feed the metrics (the share of reviews caused by validation versus policy versus low confidence). And they make a rule change testable.
e6ae82c560:
You can ask a language model to state a confidence, or to flag fields it's unsure of. That's often useful as one signal. But the exam position is clear: a self-reported number isn't calibrated until you measure it. Use it as a feature in the routing function, include it in the reliability table, and let the table tell you what it means per type.

Other signals can be cheaper, and sometimes better:

  • agreement across two independent extractions (two prompts, or two models);
  • whether the extracted value appears verbatim in the source text;
  • whether the evidence quote the model returns actually occurs in the document.

Chapter 13 covers using a second pass to verify.
30357365ff:
In a multi-agent research system, a search subagent finds sources, a reading subagent extracts findings, and a synthesis agent writes the report. Each hand-off is a summarisation step.

Prose summaries keep the claim and drop the citation. "Source: Gartner 2025 survey of 400 telecom CIOs, p. 12" becomes "surveys indicate". By the synthesis step, the report states "62% of telecom operators have deployed generative AI in customer care". Nobody can say where 62% came from, what year it describes, or whether another source said 41%.
098ea1021d: This is the same structural problem as Chapter 14: a fact passes through a lossy step. The same structural fix applies. Carry the fact in a structured form that the lossy step doesn't touch.
f22651f98b:
The reading subagent is asked to return a list of Claim objects, via a tool schema as in Chapter 12. Never a prose summary.

Publication date and collection date are separate fields. They often differ by a year or more, and that difference explains many apparent conflicts.
044fb6ee7b:
The synthesis step merges by claim_key. When sources agree, the finding is established. When numbers differ, both are kept, attributed and dated.

The rule from the objective is explicit. Don't pick one. Don't average them. Instead, annotate the conflict with sources.
0265f47c8a:
Here's example output for a contested figure: "Sources disagree: Industry Survey A reports 41% (data as of 2024-11, 1,200 operators globally); Analyst Report B reports 62% (data as of 2025-09, 400 North American CIOs)."

The dates and populations already explain most of the gap: a later collection date, and a narrower, more advanced region. The reader can judge. The report didn't hide either number.
83b33a7c81: The final report should keep three kinds of finding apart. Well-established findings have several independent sources that agree. Contested ones have sources that conflict. Single-source ones rest on one source, so treat them with care. The objective also asks you to render each content type appropriately:
28820cd99d:
A verification step can then check mechanically that every number in the report matches a claim record. This is the "scoped verify_fact tool for the synthesis agent" idea in the official sample answers.

The synthesis agent gets a narrow tool to confirm a claim against the stored records, instead of broad web search. That keeps it on its job, and it gives a check the agent can't talk its way around.
b30dde1b36:
A per-stratum accuracy estimate is only useful if it's precise enough to decide on. For a proportion, the 95% confidence interval half-width is roughly 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/n).

With 40 reviewed fields at an observed 95%, the interval is about plus or minus 7 points. You can't tell 88% from 100%. With 400 fields, it narrows to about plus or minus 2 points.

That's why the sample plan above gives small risky strata more samples than their volume share would suggest. It's also why "we checked 30 and they all looked fine" is not evidence for automation.
bb27137456: For very high accuracy targets (99%+), the counts grow quickly. That's another reason to calibrate per field. You can automate the fields where you can afford to prove the target, and keep the rest in review.
9389c7acca:
Every human correction is a labelled example. Store the reviewer's value next to the model's value, confidence and evidence. Over time this gives you a growing validation set. It tracks drift (a supplier changes its invoice layout; a new tower company sends statements in a new format). It lets you re-run threshold selection monthly. And it supplies the 2–4 targeted few-shot examples that fix specific layouts (task 4.2, Chapter 11).

Watch for one bias. Reviewed items are mostly low-confidence ones. So when you estimate the error rate of auto-posted items, use only the audit sample, which is random within each stratum.
08eafe6575:
Provenance isn't only for web research. In an enterprise, the sources are often internal: a Confluence page, a network-inventory export, a contract PDF, a data-warehouse query.

The same claim record works with different locators: page and clause for contracts, table and query text plus run time for warehouse figures, page ID and version for wiki pages.

The as-of date matters even more internally, because operational data changes daily. A report that says "1,214 sites run the legacy RAN controller" should also say "per inventory export of 2026-10-01".
7cbdbcd0aa: How fine-grained should provenance be? Finer locators make verification faster, but they cost tokens and schema complexity at every hop. Pick the coarsest level at which a reviewer can confirm a claim in under a minute.
9d33f42e1c: A useful rule: every number in an executive summary gets a quote span or a query. Descriptive context can carry page-level locators.
c028a9414d: Show fields, not documents. Present the flagged fields with the evidence quote highlighted in the source image or text. Reviewers confirm or correct. They don't re-key.
7cfb2cd52b: Record the correction as data. Store the reviewer value, model value, confidence, document type and layout, so the next calibration run uses it.
3901a93b0b: Separate audit work from review work. Don't mark audit-sample items as low-confidence in the UI. If you do, reviewers will inspect them differently, and the audit estimate becomes biased.
5592cbe5c4: Companion examples 09 to 15 build the provenance side. They're small, and each one tests one rule.
6067cc9b67:
Example 09 defines a claim record: text, value, unit, source URL and title, publication date, collection date, quote, method. It rejects a numeric claim that lacks a date or a quote.

The rule is deliberate. A number with no date can't be compared with another number. A claim with no quote can't be checked without redoing the search. Rejecting at the hand-off between subagent and synthesis puts the cost on the stage that has the source open. That's the only stage that can supply the missing field cheaply.
ee91ac69b5:
Example 10 summarises six claims two ways. The prose summary keeps the figures and loses the attribution. The structured summary keeps both. The check counts how many sources can be recovered from each: none from the prose, all from the structured form.

The point isn't that prose is always lossy; a careful writer cites. It's that nothing enforces the citation in prose, and under length pressure the citation is the first thing cut. Enforce at the format level.
66e8d6bdeb:
Example 11 groups claims about the same quantity. It marks the group conflicting when the values differ by more than a tolerance, and keeps every value with its source, date and method.

In the example, a $2.1B estimate from a label survey and a $3.4B estimate that includes generative-tool revenue are both reported, with the reason they differ. Averaging them would produce a number nobody measured. Picking the larger or the newer would hide a disagreement the reader needs to see.

The synthesis prompt should say so in so many words. The checker in example 15 enforces a different but related rule: any figure in the report must cite a known claim id.
d11e62f34d:
Example 12 classifies a finding by how independent its sources are. Two different domains agreeing on one value is established. One domain, even quoted twice, is single-source. Disagreement is contested.

The check is deliberately crude. Domains are a proxy for independence, and syndicated content or a press release repeated by many outlets is still one source. A real system needs something better. But the principle stands: count independent sources, not mentions.
31d593a26f:
Example 13 renders each kind of content in its own form. Figures become a table with source and date columns. News-like narrative becomes prose with bracketed citations. Code or configuration findings become fenced blocks with a file and line.

Matching form to content is part of the objective for a practical reason. A reader comparing five market-size estimates can do it at a glance in a table, and can't do it in a paragraph. Narrative argument, on the other hand, loses its connective tissue when forced into cells.
3d7ccd1a7a:
Example 14 compares two dates. It warns when a figure is compared with another figure from a different period.

Dates explain a surprising share of apparent contradictions: different fiscal years, a before and after of an event, a revised estimate. They also expose some real contradictions that a missing date would have hidden.
b8ceb7395e:
Example 15 passes claim records to a (scripted) synthesiser, which cites them by id. Then it runs a mechanical check over the report: every figure must carry a known claim id. The scripted model includes one invented figure, "99% [c9]", and the checker finds it.

In a production system, the same check can be a hook or a post-processing step. Combine it with a scoped verify_fact tool for the common case (Chapter 05, task 2.3). Together they turn "the model should cite" into "uncited numbers do not ship".
d1b395534a: Answer: C. A random 500 is dominated by digital invoices. So the photographed bills may be a few dozen documents, with much lower accuracy. B assumes 0.9 means 90% (or 98%) correct, which nobody measured. D may raise accuracy, but it gives no per-type evidence.
8447970fab: Answer: B. The 31% describes the low-confidence slice, not the pipeline. The confident errors that reach production aren't sampled at all. D is unstratified, and with a rare type it will measure nothing.
41276fbaf9: Answer: C. An average is a number nobody measured. Recency here would pick the lower number, which is the one with the narrower definition. Omission throws information away. The reader can resolve the conflict only if both values, their sources and the reason are visible.
bbde388543: Answer: B. The information is gone before the synthesis agent starts, so no instruction at that stage can recover it. D would produce plausible citations that aren't the real sources. That's worse than none.
646e9a005b: Answer: B. The original validation set doesn't contain the new layout (C). A threshold calibrated on old data may stay high on new wrong answers (A). Low-confidence review (D) never looks at confident errors. A random audit of the live auto-accepted population sees the shift.
2aeabcb1b7: Run an extraction function, or the Batch API for cost (Chapter 13). Build (confidence, correct) pairs per field and layout.
71943a3d02: Done when: you have a per-field, per-layout threshold table, including at least one "no threshold reaches the target" for the noisy layout. The aggregate accuracy and the worst per-layout accuracy are both reported, and they differ visibly. Auto-posted items meet the target on a held-out audit sample.
4c8ed24882: Done when: every number in the report maps to a claim record. The conflicting figures appear side by side with source, date and population. Established, contested and single-source findings sit in separate sections. And a deliberately inserted unsupported number is caught by the checker.
